entries.title: Donald Trump dismisses concerns about dangers of AI
entries.summary: The president called efforts to slow the development of artificial intelligence a "sick conspiracy," claiming they only serve China. Market leaders have warned of the dangers of the pace of the technology's development.
entries.content:
September 14, 2026

The president called efforts to slow the development of artificial intelligence a "sick conspiracy," claiming they only serve China. Market leaders have warned of the dangers of the pace of the technology's development.

US President Donald Trump has called concerns that artificial intelligence is progressing too quickly a "SICK conspiracy."

Trump's statement followed calls by tech leaders such as Anthropic's Dario Amodei and OpenAI's Sam Altman for more governmental regulation of AI. In recent months, several incidents have highlighted the risk that AI agents could go rogue.

What Trump said about AI 'guardrails'

"The only control or ‘guardrails' that AI needs is a STRONG AND SMART (High IQ!) PRESIDENT, and the U.S.A. has that, in spades!" Trump posted on his Truth Social account.

Trump added that his administration has already prevented Anthropic from "doing bad, or potentially bad" things with the technology.

The Pentagon previously tried to brand Anthropic's models a security risk and posed a temporary ban on one of its more advanced models.

"There is a SICK conspiracy going on against AI and Data Centers, and the only one that is happy about it is China," Trump wrote.

Anthropic boss Amodei warned against uncontrolled global AI development over the weekend saying that there's a risk of AI-led agents taking over the entire internet within six to 12 months. Microsoft published its own code of conduct to ensure human control over AI.

This led to AI stocks falling worldwide, including those of chip maker Nvidia (3.5%) and Elon Musk's SpaceX (1.7%).

Edited by: Kieran Burke

entries.title: Yemen's Houthis attack Saudis, seize crucial Red Sea islands
entries.summary: Iran-backed Houthi rebels have tightened their grip on a key shipping route, capturing two strategic Red Sea islands. The closure of another global transport route is the latest ripple effect of the US war with Iran.
entries.content:
Middle East

Yemen's Houthis attack Saudis, seize crucial Red Sea islands

September 14, 2026

Iran-backed Houthi rebels have tightened their grip on a key shipping route, capturing two strategic Red Sea islands. The closure of another global transport route is the latest ripple effect of the US war with Iran.

Iranian-backed Houthi rebels on Monday announced they had captured Greater and Lesser Hanish Island in the southern Red Sea.

The move bolsters the group's ability to choke traffic in another key global maritime shipping route as the ripple-effect of the war in Iran grows.

The strategic advance comes as Saudi-backed Yemeni forces try to regain territory recently lost near the Bab el-Mandab Strait, an important alternative to the Strait of Hormuz — which Iran has held closed since US President Donald Trump began bombing the Islamic Republic on February 28.

The closure of the Hormuz Strait, through which roughly one-fifth of the world's oil passed before the US began hostilities, has led to a global economic and energy emergency, driving up prices around the world and forcing petro-monarchy Saudi Arabia to move its oil exports through Bab el-Mandab.

But the Houthis have declared a maritime blockade on Saudi Arabia and last week seized strategic Mayun Island and the Red Sea port of Mokha, cutting off the alternative route.

The capture of Greater and Lesser Hanish now puts even more pressure on Saudi shipments and thus global oil supplies and prices.

Beyond putting the squeeze on Saudi Arabia — the Houthis' proxy enemy for backing the internationally recognized government in the Yemen's reignited civil war — it could also provide Iran added leverage in defending itself against the US.

Houthi offensive continues to escalate as Iran war expands

The Houthis pressed on with their offensive Monday, launching missile and drone attacks on Saudi military targets.

A spokesman for the group said the strikes had caused "significant damage" and had come in response to "more than 300 [Saudi] airstrikes in [Yemen over] the past five days."

Despite being a longtime backer of the Houthis as part of its anti-Israel "axis of resistance," Tehran has denied any involvement in Yemen's revived civil war.

"Iran does not interfere in Yemeni affairs," said Tehran's Foreign Ministry on Monday, with spokesman Esmaeil Baqaei telling reporters the Houthis are "entirely independent actors who make their decisions based on their own interests."

Yemen's civil war — dormant for four years until the conflict in Iran broke out — began in 2014, when Houthi rebels seized large parts of northern Yemen, including the capital Sanaa, and forced the government to flee to Aden in the south.

In 2015, Saudi Arabia led a military coalition aiding the government, launching wave after wave of airstrikes as the conflict escalated into one of the worst humanitarian disasters in the world.

Concerning situation for US and its Saudi, Gulf State allies

On Monday, Admiral Brad Cooper of US Central Command (CENTCOM) was in Jeddah to discuss "the latest developments in the region" with Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman.

US news site Axios reports that Cooper has been in the kingdom since Thursday, dealing with urgent coordination meetings as the situation in the Red Sea escalates.

US media outlets reported last week that President Trump had rejected a request by the crown prince for the US to directly intervene.

Despite turning down the request to unleash US firepower, Trump reportedly agreed to provide intelligence sharing and targeting assistance.

Iran blames Saudi Arabia for stalling Hormuz talks

Iran on Monday accused Saudi Arabia of delaying talks aimed at reopening the Strait of Hormuz.

Foreign Ministry spokesman Baghaei called a meeting set to take place in Oman, a "real opportunity" to restore security in the region and added that an agreement between Iran and Oman on opening the passage had been finalized and would be announced later.

Saudi Arabia reportedly has concerns over the lasting implications of a deal for the Strait of Hormuz and how it might negatively impact Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC) countries.

Tehran says Riyadh is using Yemen as a "pretext" to delay talks on how the Strait will be governed now that the status quo has been upended by the US.

Currently, the only secure routes allowing Saudi Arabia to deliver its oil to Asian markets are via the Suez Canal or around South Africa's Cape of Good Hope.

On Monday, China's Foreign Ministry called attacks on Saudi energy infrastructure "unacceptable," saying Beijing is "deeply concerned" about further escalation.

Edited by: Kieran Burke

entries.title: Ukraine, Russia set for new round of US-mediated talks
entries.summary: New trilateral talks between Ukraine, Russia and the US could begin in October, according to Kyiv and Moscow. Few expect a breakthrough, but Ukraine is seeking a partial de-escalation to help it get through the winter.
entries.content:
Ukraine

Ukraine, Russia set for new round of US-mediated talks

September 14, 2026

New trilateral talks between Ukraine, Russia and the US could begin in October, according to Kyiv and Moscow. Few expect a breakthrough, but Ukraine is seeking a partial de-escalation to help it get through the winter.

Ukraine and Russia have signaled their readiness to resume trilateral talks under US mediation.

"We're preparing. For October," said Kyrylo Budanov, head of the Ukrainian president's office.

Similar signals came from Moscow: "We do not rule out such a possibility. We are talking about the foreseeable future," Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said.

US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner aimed to revive trilateral talks to end Russia's war in Ukraine, visiting Moscow and Kyiv in the first week of September.

The last round of trilateral talks took place in January and February 2026 in Abu Dhabi and Geneva, without producing a breakthrough, as the issue of territory control in eastern Ukraine remained unresolved.

Territory remains a difficult subject

Vladimir Putin still demands more territory than Russia currently controls, Kushner confirmed on September 12, speaking online at the YES security conference in Kyiv.

"President Putin [has] laid out his line of what he wants to achieve. If Ukraine wanted to withdraw to that line, then obviously we have the rest of the deal set up and put together. Ukraine right now does not want to do that," the US envoy said.

The Ukrainian government has indicated it is willing to freeze the fighting along the current frontline in exchange for security guarantees. Such a step could be supported by 60% of Ukrainians, according to a poll by the Kyiv International Institute of Sociology conducted in summer 2026. A similar majority of respondents rejected giving up territory that Russia hasn't been able to conquer. 33% said Ukraine should give up territory that Putin demands.

Russia's air superiority is a problem for Ukraine

Few expect a breakthrough anytime soon.

"For there to be a negotiated end to the war, there has to be parity. Right now, there's a stalemate on the front lines and not much is changing there, but in the air war, unfortunately, Russia currently has a significant advantage," Volodymyr Fesenko, a Kyiv-based political scientist, told DW.

Ukraine is running low on interceptors for Russian ballistic missiles. Russia has also stepped up attacks with new jet-powered drones, which fly faster than older gasoline-powered models and are harder to intercept.

Russian airstrikes are increasingly targeting Ukraine's economy, including warehouses, energy facilities, gas stations and railway infrastructure.

The Kremlin has accused Ukraine of opening a "Pandora's box" by targeting Russia's economy and fuel and energy facilities with deep strikes since the summer. Ukraine says the attacks are intended to force Russia to the negotiating table.

Ukraine is worrying about the winter

Ukraine's supporters say Kyiv's strategy is working.

"The escalation ... is not a problem. It's a sign of success," said Jonathan Powell, the United Kingdom's National Security Adviser, speaking at the Yalta European Strategy conference in Kyiv on September 11. "Of course [Putin] doesn't go straight to negotiations, he tries to escalate in the ways that he can."

The West must "keep its foot on the gas" to make Putin negotiate in earnest, Powell said.

Such optimism contrasts with concerns in Ukraine about the upcoming winter. In 2025, Russian attacks on energy infrastructure caused extended blackouts and left people without heating in freezing temperatures.

"We anticipate a very difficult winter in terms of both critical infrastructure, which is being destroyed every day by Russian attacks, but also in terms of overall economic conditions in the country," said Ukraine's Economy Minister, Oleksandr Kravchenko.

Zelenskyy calls for partial de-escalation

Russia rejected the idea of a ceasefire during the upcoming talks. Ukraine is now calling for a de-escalation of attacks on energy infrastructure and the unblocking of grain exports via the Black Sea instead.

"What can bring us to any kind of negotiations? So, energy and grain. This is step number one. What we can achieve," Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelenskyy told DW in an interview aired on September 12.

Political scientist Fesenko says an agreement on grain exports could prove the easier task: "In the Black Sea, both Ukraine and Russia are facing major problems. Grain exports have been blocked; ports have been shut down and therefore both sides have a stake in the matter."

An energy truce, however, remains elusive, as Ukraine's vulnerability in the winter gives Putin leverage he would not give up easily, Fesenko said.

At the same time, the US is increasing pressure on Ukraine to halt its attacks on Russian energy facilities.

"Mr. Zelenskyy has to do one thing: He has to ‌stop ⁠knocking out diesel fuel in Russia," Donald Trump said on Sunday, September 13. "There are plenty of other targets. Don't hit diesel fuel. That's hurting the world."

Kremlin rejected Zelenskyy-Putin meeting

The Kremlin has already rejected another of Zelenskyy's proposals: a meeting between the Ukrainian and Russian leaders in December on the sidelines of the G20 summit in Miami.

"Putin doesn't want to negotiate with Zelenskyy. It's been obvious since last year that he wants to reach an agreement with Trump," said Fesenko. "If Trump insists, Putin may agree to a meeting between the three leaders. But he has no intention of negotiating with Zelenskyy."

If negotiations start in October as expected, negotiating teams rather than the leaders themselves will conduct them. But Ukraine insists that only the presidents can decide the territorial issue.

"The territorial question remains a pressing one... Complex issues such as this are only resolved at the level of leaders," Zelenskyy said during the US envoys' visit to Kyiv.

Edited by: Carla Bleiker

entries.title: Women's Basketball World Cup: Can Germany harness a boom?
entries.summary: Germany thrilled fans at the Women's Basketball World Cup. But even if this sparked a boom in the women's game, the infrastructure simply isn't ready for it.
entries.content:
September 14, 2026

Germany thrilled fans at the Women's Basketball World Cup. But even if this sparked a boom in the women's game, the infrastructure simply isn't ready for it.

The world's best players showcased their sport at the Women's Basketball World Cup in Berlin, which wrapped up on September 13.

Germany, led by Leonie Fiebich and Nyara, improved with every game throughout the preliminary and intermediate round of the 10-day tournament. In the quarterfinals, Germany beat European champions Belgium, delivering what was arguably their best-ever performance.

The final weekend though, revealed the team still isn't quite ready to compete with the world's elite over a full 40 minutes. Germany lost to France in the semifinals before losing to Spain in the match for third place. Despite their disappointment, the Germans still saw the tournament as a huge success.

"We simply aren't good enough yet," said Fiebich after the Spain match.

"We played the tournament with a lot of euphoria and beat the European champions, Belgium. But it's hard to keep overperforming. Still, we will get better."

The World Cup marked a climax of the positive development seen in German women's basketball in recent years. In 2024, the team qualified for the Olympic Games for the first time, where the women also won a surprising gold in the 3x3 basketball. At the 2025 EuroBasket, Germany's women finished fifth. The next women's EuroBasket is next year and if Germany qualify, they should be medal contenders.

"I think it's important to harness the pain the players are feeling right now," Germany head coach Olaf Lange said.

"Because in our day-to-day work over the coming months and years, we need to improve individually. That requires a lot of motivation, and this pain acts as fuel for improvement."

The support from Germany fans could hardly have been greater. A total of around 230,000 tickets were sold for the World Cup and although visiting fans were present, the crowds were made up primarily of Germans.

Only three play for German clubs

While the national team is just a few steps away from establishing itself among the world's elite, Germany's top women's basketball league (DBBL) lags well behind the international competition.

Most players from the World Cup squad play abroad. Fiebich, Nyara Sabally and her sister Satou, who missed the tournament due to injury, as well as Luisa Geiselsöder and Frieda Bühner, play in the WNBA. Team captain Marie Gülich is moving to a club in Australia after the World Cup, having previously played in Taiwan. Emily Bessoir, Lina Sontag, and Alexis Peterson-Smalls play in Spain. Clara Bielefeld currently plays US college basketball.

Only three Germany players; Alexandra Wilke, Emma Eichmeyer, and Britta Daub, play for DBBL clubs, although both Eichmeyer and Daub have previously played abroad.

In Germany, they simply can't earn a living from playing basketball. Wilke, for example, works as a teacher at a secondary school.

DBBL level 'semi-professional'

Lange, who was a coach in the league from 1995 to 2002, describes it as "semi-professional," and says it has gone downhill since he left.

"Back then, the top clubs had better structures than they do today—and we are in 2026. That says it all. Things are really going backwards," he lamented during his post-tournament press conference.

"I have to ensure that our top players go abroad. As long as nothing changes in the league, it will be difficult to sustain this success."

Professionalization efforts

Changes are needed to ensure the national team's continued success. Ireti Amojo took over as DBBL president in March. The former Germany player is a TV pundit and podcaster and has also worked in management of the women's program of top men's club ALBA Berlin. She has introduced several measures aimed to professionalize conditions at DBBL clubs.

"We aim to hire full-time youth development coaches. We also want to increase arena capacities," Amojo told daily newspaper TAZ prior to the World Cup.

"Currently, some venues hold a maximum of 600 spectators, and if interest grows – as it is now – we will need larger arenas."

'Too late to capitalize on a World Cup boom'

However, the top division is not the whole story; even if the Women's Basketball World Cup were to trigger a surge of young girls taking up the game in Germany, most clubs would be ill-prepared to handle them. This is partly due to a shortage of coaches, but also because there is a lack of basketball facilities, making court time scarce.

"We should have started five years ago so that we could say now: 'We are capitalizing on the momentum of the World Cup and ensuring that all these kids who have become basketball fans can play the sport in clubs across Germany,'" Amojo told Magenta Sport after the World Cup final.

"We are too late. We lack the structures to harness this interest and provide all the children fascinated by basketball with the opportunity, under perfect training conditions, to develop into the next Leonie Fiebich or Nyara Sabally."

Still, Amojo thinks the World Cup may just prove to be a much-needed spark for future development.

"It was the kind of proof we all needed, because people are quick to dismiss it, claiming that no one in Germany is interested in women's basketball. Now we've seen that people in Germany are interested in women's basketball," she said.

"We already have a few levers we want to use to work on the structures. And this certainly shouldn't be the end of things."

This article was originally written in German.

Edited by: Jonathan Harding

entries.title: IPO 'for the people' is out of reach for many in Nigeria
entries.summary: Dangote seeks $1.6 billion from investors to finance a $14.3 billion expansion and thus double the oil refinery's capacity. The offer could give millions of Nigerians a stake in the company. But who can truly afford it?
entries.content:
Nigeria

IPO 'for the people' is out of reach for many in Nigeria

September 14, 2026

Dangote seeks $1.6 billion from investors to finance a $14.3 billion expansion and thus double the oil refinery's capacity. The offer could give millions of Nigerians a stake in the company. But who can truly afford it?

The industrialist Aliko Dangote is turning to Nigerians to help finance the next growth phase of his oil refinery: The richest man in Africa announced that he is seeking to attract about $1.6 billion (€1.4 billion) by going public.

This initial public offering of Dangote Industries is intended to help support a $14.3 billion expansion, which would more than double the refinery's production capacity. In absolute numbers, it would increase capacity from 700,000 barrels per day (bpd) to 1.4 million bpd.

It would also include new petrochemical and refining units designed to reduce Nigeria's reliance on imports of some petrochemical products while also allowing the plant to produce different grades of diesel.

This plan would make the refinery one of the largest single-site refining complexes in the world.

Dangote's ambitious plans also include the launch of a processing plant in Kenya to extend his reach from the Atlantic to the Indian Ocean, which is planned to be launched in partnership with governments in eastern Africa.

African success story

Since it began operations in 2024, the Dangote Petroleum Refinery has started to reshape Nigeria's fuel market, and has become one of the few businesses in the world to benefit from the ongoing supply disruptions caused by the war in Iran.

The refinery has become an important supplier of petrol and other fuels domestically and abroad; in fact, it made Nigeria a net exporter of refined fuel for the first time after reaching its full capacity in early 2026.

The refinery reported making an after-tax profit of $1.82 ​billion in the first half ​of 2026, following ⁠a $476 million loss for all of 2025.

Things appear to be on the up-and-up for Dangote — so, why is the company seeking public investment now?

Why go public?

Ayodele Oni, an energy analyst and partner with the Bloomfield Law Practice in Lagos, told DW that the public offering could be a "game changer," as it alters the role of who could stand to benefit from Dangote's expansion drive.

Oni said equity invested by potentially millions of Nigerian and international shareholders would shield the corporation from having to rely solely on expensive dollar debt "with permanent Naira capital, which matches a business now earning heavily in Naira."

This could also unlock additional long-term investment as any "listed company answers to ... its shareholders every quarter."



"That transparency is precisely what long-term lenders and international partners want to see before the next billion is committed," Oni said.

He said this would turn into a sustainable model for Dangote, as the approach would be designed to permanently "lower its cost of capital for every future phase."

For 'the people'

Oni summarized the potential of the deal by referring to it as a restructuring of both who bears the risk — and who stands to share with the reward, with "the people" being the greatest beneficiaries of the IPO, at least to his mind.

Opening up the ownership of the refinery business to ordinary Nigerians does not automatically mean that many can afford it, however.

The pricing of the initial offering is indeed priced at an affordable 525 Naira (€0.34/$0.39) a piece for each of the 4.1 billion ordinary shares, and a minimum of just 10 shares.

At the signing ceremony in Lagos, Dangote said the company was trying to "make sure that the majority of … our drivers, our cook, our servants, our managers, everybody will have an opportunity to have a stake in the refinery."

Deep inequality, deeper pockets

In a country where almost two-thirds of the population is struggling with extreme poverty, according to Nigeria's National Bureau of Statistics, that figure can translate into 10% of the minimum wage — for people who are fortunate enough to have a job.

Entry-level employees and workers who perform menial tasks at Dangote are fortunate enough to earn almost four times the minimum wage in Nigeria, according to media reports — though this still translates to only about $150 a month in a country that has been witnessing steep inflation, especially in petrol prices. For most, seeing any personal benefit by investing in Nigeria's oil remains a pipe dream.

Charles Asiegbu, a policy and economic analyst who has worked as a consultant for various Nigerian organizations, told DW that Dangote's description of the offer as "for the people" could still qualify as a "psychological masterstroke" for those who can afford to invest.

Asiegbu said broader ownership could bring a large number of Nigerians into one consolidated platform, changing how they view the refinery.

"With millions as shareholders, it would shift from a private enterprise to a national asset in the public consciousness," Asiegbu said.

IPO excites investors

Nigerians who can afford to invest in Dangote appear to quickly be adopting that mindset.

Olamilekan Oladehinde, a Nigerian retail investor, told DW that he is "excited" to partake in the launch and buy shares. He said Dangote was now much more than just a private enterprise: It has become a key national asset that addresses direct social problems in Nigeria — including fuel shortages.

"They're trying to expand, and that's something I am very proud and happy to identify with," Oladehinde said. "The fact that it's also owned by a Nigerian makes me more than happy, and that's why I will be buying a stake in the company," he said about the richest man in Africa.

Risks and opportunities

Oladehinde said he had no concerns about investing in Dangote — despite the fact that various market experts have cautioned investors to be mindful of potential risks, especially because refining is a cyclical business.

Oni said Dangote was riding a wave during the current situation across the Middle East; however, fortunes could change — especially when the tensions around the Strait of Hormuz eventually ease. A return to steep competition in oil prices from those Middle Eastern countries could then saturate markets.

Dangote's strengths were a mitigating factor, Oni said: "The Middle East disruption showed that a refinery on [Nigeria's] Atlantic coast can supply Europe and the Americas faster than the Gulf can — and, at 700,000 bpd, the plant has already proven the model, so the expansion is about scale on an existing site, which is the cheapest capacity anyone can build."

Oladehinde said this was exactly the outlook that he will be betting on. "I believe the time has come for us," he said. "We can't lose this the momentum."

Edited by: Sertan Sanderson

entries.title: Germany news: Merz urges CDU discipline as pressure grows
entries.summary: Chancellor Friedrich Merz has urged his party to stay disciplined as pressure grows over his leadership. Meanwhile, Germany's homeownership rate has fallen to its lowest level in 20 years. DW has the latest.
entries.content:
Germany

Germany news: Merz urges CDU discipline as pressure grows

Published September 14, 2026last updated September 14, 2026

Chancellor Friedrich Merz has urged his party to stay disciplined as pressure grows over his leadership. Meanwhile, Germany's homeownership rate has fallen to its lowest level in 20 years. DW has the latest.

Skip next section What you need to know

What you need to know

  • Friedrich Merz has urged his party to stay focused as criticism of his leadership grows after the CDU’s defeat to the AfD in Saxony-Anhalt
  • Coalition partners and opposition parties are now openly questioning what happens next
  • Germany's homeownership rate has fallen to 43.5%, its lowest level in 20 years
  • A study blames high construction costs, higher interest rates and housing policy

Here is a roundup of top stories from and about Germany on Monday, September 14, 2026:

Tired of missing our real-time updates? Click here to add DW as a Preferred Source on Google.

Skip next section Suspended sentence for priest in possession of child pornography

Suspended sentence for priest in possession of child pornography

A Catholic priest from North Rhine-Westphalia has received a suspended 14-month jail sentence after being found guilty of possessing of some 24,000 data files containing images and footage of sexual abuse of children and youths.

The district court in Waldbröl, a rural area to the east of Cologne and Bonn in the Westerwald forest, found the man guilty on Monday. 

The verdict is subject to appeal.

The defendant had pleaded guilty to all charges, leading to a comparatively quick court process.

As well as the suspended sentence, the man was ordered to pay €10,000 (roughly $11,500) to a local facility providing advice and counsel to those affected by sexualized, psychological and physical abuse.

He was also ordered to complete a therapy course that he had already begun.

The Cologne diocese, of which Waldbröl is a part, had already suspended the priest from various activities after the allegations became public knowledge. Among other things he was stopped from working with minors. 

He's also subject to church disciplinary proceedings. These had been put on hold pending the outcome of the court case.

Skip next section Police called to reprimand man painting house in 'just his shoes'

Police called to reprimand man painting house in 'just his shoes'

Police on duty in Kaiserslautern had a more colorful callout than they might have bargained for over the weekend.

Police said on Monday that early on Saturday evening, they had received calls from residents displeased by a man painting a facade in his driveway. 

They took exception to the fact that their neighbor was "wearing just his shoes," as police put it, during his travails.

"After officers brought to his attention that he was creating a disturbance in the community with his actions, the 64-year-old became intransigent," police said.

"Only after an explicit order did he put some trousers on. He was told that his behavior constituted a breach of the peace and that he should reckon with a criminal complaint."

Skip next section Fuel prices hit record high, ADAC considers levels unjustified

Fuel prices hit record high, ADAC considers levels unjustified

Prices for drivers at German filling stations hit the highest levels on record for gasoline on Sunday, while diesel was just shy of April's record prices.

The nationwide average for the cheapest E10 unleaded variant hit €2.27 per liter on Sunday. That equates to roughly $9.92 per US gallon.

Diesel was slightly shy of its record level but still rose to €2.40 per liter, or $10.48 per US gallon.

Germany's largest motoring club the ADAC said that "given the still-rising oil prices it can be assumed that slight increases in the daily average prices for Super E10 and diesel will emerge" on Monday.  

Prices for gasoline and diesel have risen quite sharply in September, and more generally since the German government's temporary tax relief introduced in response to the war in Iran expired at the end of June.

Developments in the Gulf have been driving the price upwards, despite claims to the contrary from under-fire US President Donald Trump on Monday.

The ADAC, which is frequently critical of the country's fuel providers and their pricing policies, argued that geopolitics alone still did not explain the latest hikes.

"In the view of the ADAC, the oil price and the euro-dollar exchange rate only partly explain the current price levels at the petrol pumps," the ADAC wrote. "What's particularly noticeable is how Super E10 keeps hitting new record highs, even though crude oil prices are far adrift of their previous highs. For consumers this development is difficult to explain."

The ADAC called on refining and fuel selling companies to be more transparent in their pricing practices.

Skip next section Light aircraft crashes south of Mönchengladbach, 3 killed

Light aircraft crashes south of Mönchengladbach, 3 killed

A light aircraft crashed in a field in Erkelenz in the western state of North Rhine-Westphalia on Monday. 

Police in nearby Heinsberg said three people were killed in the crash; nobody on board the small Cessna survived.

Police said the crash happened before noon in a rural area south of Mönchengladbach and that they were still working to identify the victims.

Firefighters and police were at the scene on Monday. The German body responsible to investigating air traffic accidents had started an invesigation, which police said was liable to take some time.

Skip next section SPD says coalition is not dependent on Merz staying chancellor

SPD says coalition is not dependent on Merz staying chancellor

Senior figures in the center-left Social Democratic Party (SPD) have expressed growing concern about the turmoil inside Chancellor Friedrich Merz's conservative Christian Democratic Union (CDU).

They also made clear that their party's participation in the coalition is not dependent on Merz's remaining chancellor.

SPD parliamentary manager Dirk Wiese said there was an impression that "nerves are a little frayed within the CDU" and urged the coalition partner to regain its focus and move ahead with reforms agreed by the government.

Asked whether those reforms necessarily had to be implemented with Merz as chancellor, Wiese declined to commit himself, saying instead that Merz needed to adopt a different tone.

SPD parliamentary deputy leader Siemtje Möller was more explicit. She said her party's participation in the governing coalition was not tied to Merz personally.

Skip next section Merz urges CDU unity as pressure mounts

Merz urges CDU unity as pressure mounts

German Chancellor Friedrich Merz has urged his center-right Christian Democratic Union (CDU) to remain disciplined as criticism of his leadership grows following the party's election defeat in Saxony-Anhalt.

Speaking at an international Arctic policy meeting in Rovaniemi, Finland, Merz said Germany was playing an important role in determining "the fate of the European continent," particularly on security policy.

He said he was therefore trying to convince "my colleagues, my friends, my party, my parliamentary group that this is much more important than some of the domestic political debates we are currently having."

"I understand this domestic political debate," Merz said.

Merz has faced mounting criticism within the CDU since the party's poor performance in the Saxony-Anhalt state election, with some members openly discussing whether he should be replaced.

Several prominent CDU politicians nevertheless backed the chancellor on Monday.

"I still believe in Friedrich Merz," CDU budget policy spokesman Matthias Middelberg told the broadcaster Deutschlandfunk, calling the leadership debate "unnecessary."

Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul said Merz could "always rely on the support of the governing parliamentary groups and his Cabinet," describing the government as "really very stable."

Skip next section Green leader tells Merz coalition: 'Get your s--- together'

Green leader tells Merz coalition: 'Get your s--- together'

Green Party co-leader Felix Banaszak has told Chancellor Friedrich Merz's government to "get your s--- together" amid growing speculation over a possible change of chancellor.

"I am extremely irritated by all the speculation that is coming from everywhere," Banaszak said in Berlin on Monday. "And my expectation is very clear: Get your s--- together. We are living in such dramatic times."

Banaszak said that, though he had not voted for Merz, the chancellor and his coalition had been elected and had a responsibility to govern the country.

The Green politician pointed to discussions about minority governments, the possible dismissal of ministers from the center-left Social Democratic Party (SPD) and scenarios involving an early replacement of Merz.

He said the debates suggested that Merz and the leadership of his center-right Christian Democratic Union (CDU) were losing control both of the coalition and of discussions within their own party.

"That is not a good sign," Banaszak said.

Skip next section Germany’s largest union calling for nationwide protests over auto sector job cuts

Germany’s largest union calling for nationwide protests over auto sector job cuts

The German union IG Metall is calling for demonstrations in more than 200 locations across the country on September 21. The demonstrations will be held to protest job cuts and other demands being made of workers in the auto industry. 

Christiane Benner, leader of IG Metall, said most of the sector's crisis is falling on employees. "We are currently witnessing an unprecedented attack on workers in the auto industry," she said, adding that the union's main concern is the risk of losing the 35-hour workweek, a standard in the German auto sector. 

Employers' demands in times of crisis

Due to the current challenges facing the sector, automakers are proposing an increase to a 40-hour workweek with no wage adjustments.

Jens Schäfer, chairman of the ZF Automotive Works Council in Hanover, said this would mean five additional hours of work without extra pay.

"That's driving colleagues crazy," he said, adding that it would also lead to more job losses.

Benner said workers have already made sacrifices, including concessions in collective bargaining agreements and pay concessions worth billions of euros, while companies continue to pay dividends and management has faced no consequences for past mistakes.

IG Metall's goal is to mobilize more than 100,000 people on September 21.

Skip next section Merz congratulates Zverev on US Open victory

Merz congratulates Zverev on US Open victory

German Chancellor Friedrich Merz has congratulated Alexander Zverev on winning the US Open, his second Grand Slam title of the season.

The German defeated Ben Shelton 6-3, 7-6 (7-2), 5-7, 6-2 in Sunday's final in New York.

"First Paris, now New York: Heartfelt congratulations, dear Alex Zverev, on the well-deserved US Open victory and your second Grand Slam title in a season. Stellar performance!" Merz wrote on X.

Zverev also won the French Open in June. Merz called him after that victory to offer his congratulations.

Skip next section Nearly half of German schoolchildren report sleep problems

Nearly half of German schoolchildren report sleep problems

Almost half of schoolchildren in Germany say they regularly have problems sleeping, according to a new survey published by health insurer DAK-Gesundheit.

The survey found that 46% of pupils in grades 5 to 10 experience sleep problems at least once a week, up from 36% in the 2019/2020 school year.

At the same time, 69% said they felt drained or exhausted at least once a week. Three years ago, the figure was 52%.

Michael Hubmann, president of Germany's professional association of pediatricians, pointed to excessive media use as one factor behind the increase in sleep and exhaustion problems.

"Children and adolescents who use social media until late in the evening or consume disturbing videos triggered by algorithms are being kept from healthy sleep," he said.

DAK chief executive Andreas Storm warned that persistent exhaustion and sleep problems could make it harder for children to learn successfully.

"Anyone who is already exhausted at a young age or even suffers from sleep disorders and does not know how to deal with such pressures has worse conditions for successful learning," he said.

Skip next section Germany to order 4th new signals intelligence ship

Germany to order 4th new signals intelligence ship

German Defense Minister Boris Pistorius has announced that Germany will acquire a fourth signals intelligence ship.

"These ships can hear and see what others cannot. They are our eyes and ears at sea. They perceive and analyze a vast range of signals and sounds," the minister said during a keel-laying ceremony for the third ship of this type to be built by the German company Rheinmetall.

The acquisition is part of a budget proposal that is pending parliamentary approval, he added.

Pistorius also said the ships were essential for providing situational awareness and enabling precise maneuvering in times of increasing insecurity.

The new class of ships are expected to be delivered to the German Navy from 2029.

Skip next section Germany sees slowing economic momentum in 3rd quarter

Germany sees slowing economic momentum in 3rd quarter

The German Ministry of Economy says the country is experiencing an economic slowdown at the beginning of the third quarter.

"The economic boom in energy-intensive industries, which was driven by increased foreign demand in the wake of the conflict in the Middle East, appears to be slowing down," the ministry said in its monthly report.

High energy costs have caused domestic consumption to decline considerably, a trend also driven by the conflict, the report said.

Skip next section Berlin businesswoman charged over alleged spying for Russia

Berlin businesswoman charged over alleged spying for Russia

German federal prosecutors have charged a 57-year-old Berlin businesswoman with carrying out intelligence activities for Russia.

Ilona W., who holds German and Ukrainian citizenship, is accused of working for the intelligence service of a foreign power, the Federal Prosecutor's Office said.

She was arrested on January 21 and remains in pre-trial detention.

Read more about this story here.

Skip next section Germany's homeownership rate falls to 20-year low

Germany's homeownership rate falls to 20-year low

Fewer people in Germany are living in homes they own, with the country's homeownership rate falling to its lowest level in 20 years, according to a study.

The rate now stands at 43.5%, the Augsburger Allgemeine newspaper reported, citing research by the Pestel Institute.

Institute director Matthias Günther said Germany ranked last in Europe for homeownership.

Günther pointed to high construction costs, higher interest rates and housing policy over recent years.

"Even where property prices are stagnating or falling, even dual-income households on average salaries are barely able to afford a home of their own," he said.

According to the study, residential construction costs have risen by 160% since 2000, compared with a 64% increase in overall consumer prices.

Younger people are bearing much of the impact, Günther said. Almost three-quarters of people aged 25 to 45 currently live in rented accommodation, the study found.

Skip next section Germany and Hungary seek reset after political change

Germany and Hungary seek reset after political change

Germany and Hungary have "an enormous amount of catching up to do" in their diplomatic relations, German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul has said.

The politician is visiting Hungary as the first German foreign minister to do so in almost seven years.

"Hungary and Germany are opening a new chapter together," Wadephul said before his departure.

He said the political change in Hungary offered an opportunity to rebuild relations "at great speed" on a foundation of mutual trust and reliability.

Hungary's new government had launched important reforms within a short period, he said, adding that a return to the rule of law and implementation of EU requirements were good news both for Europe and for Hungarians.

The nationalist Fidesz party of former Prime Minister Viktor Orban was voted out of office in April. Orban had faced years of criticism from the EU over concerns about democracy and the rule of law.

Since May, conservative Prime Minister Peter Magyar has led a new pro-European government.

Wadephul said predictable rules and the rule of law were important not only for public confidence but also for companies considering investment.

"If fair and reliable competitive conditions once again apply to companies from all EU member states, Hungary's economy will benefit considerably," he said.

German companies already account for around 250,000 jobs in Hungary, according to Wadephul.

A delegation of German business representatives is accompanying him to Budapest to discuss what further steps are needed.

entries.title: Ukraine: AfD questions German aid, Berlin remains committed
entries.summary: Emboldened by its win in Saxony-Anhalt, the far-right Alternative for Germany wants the government to change its Ukraine and Russia policies. Berlin is staying the course, but support is fading — especially in the east.
entries.content:
Germany

AfD puts pressure on German aid to Ukraine

September 14, 2026

Emboldened by its win in Saxony-Anhalt, the far-right Alternative for Germany wants the government to change its Ukraine and Russia policies. Berlin is staying the course, but support is fading — especially in the east.

German Chancellor Friedrich Merz is standing firm on military aid for Ukraine in its war with Russia.

"We support Ukraine, and we will continue to support her, because she is also defending our freedom," Merz said on September 9 during a debate in the Bundestag, Germany's lower house of parliament.

He was reacting to Alternative for Germany (AfD) co-leader Alice Weidel, who had urged him to "finally start pushing for peace talks, like the US is doing."

US President Donald Trump has indicated that he would make far-reaching concessions to Russia at such negotiations; critics in Germany have described that as dictated peace.

On the topic of high energy prices in Germany, Weidel said, "We need cheap natural gas from Russia. That is what we will work toward."

She insinuated that the Ukrainian government was responsible for blowing up the Nord Stream gas pipelines between Russia and Germany in September 2022. "They continue to reward the suspected masterminds of the attack in Kyiv with billion-dollar payments at the expense of Germany." A Ukrainian sabotage team is suspected to be behind the attack.

How pro-Russia the AfD is, despite its invasion of Ukraine, was shown clearly by its lawmaker Jürgen Koegel during the debate. He spoke of "valued President Vladimir Putin," who posed no threat of war to NATO.

East-west division in Germany over Ukraine aid

The AfD's position on the war in Ukraine is nothing new. However, since winning the state parliament election in Saxony-Anhalt on September 6 by a large margin, gaining almost 44% of the vote, it has expressed it even more vehemently.

Combining the votes for the AfD, the socialist Left Party and the populist Sahra Wagenknecht Alliance (BSW), about 60% of voters in Saxony-Anhalt chose parties that either oppose support for Ukraine or are skeptical of it.

According to one survey, citizens' concerns about peace in Europe influenced their votes. Those surveyed named this topic as their second-most important, after "social security" and far ahead of "immigration" or "environment and climate."

In addition, there is the result of an ARD Deutschlandtrend survey conducted shortly before the election. It showed an east-west divide on the question of military support for Ukraine. About 39% of western Germans (from the area which was West Germany prior to reunification) thought military assistance went too far, while it was 54% for eastern Germans — that is, people who live in the area which used to be the communist German Democratic Republic (GDR/DDR).

"The course that the German federal government is taking on Ukraine does not have majority support in the east," Johannes Varwick, a political scientist at the Martin Luther University Halle-Wittenberg in Saxony-Anhalt, told DW.

"I would not describe that as 'pro-Russia'; it comes from the desire to focus more on diplomacy rather than delivering ever more weapons to fuel a war which Ukraine cannot win."

Fear in Germany of Russian threats

On September 2, the German government blamed Russia for a failed attack with an armed drone in early August at Leipzig airport, a key hub for military aid to Ukraine.

Putin spoke of a "grave error," Russian Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov even called the accusation the "start of a real war." The exchange of verbal blows marked a new level of escalation in an already tense relationship.

According to the latest ARD Deutschlandtrend survey, most Germans (56%) see themselves currently either strongly or very strongly threatened by Russia. But it also showed that eastern Germans and AfD voters feel less threatened by Russia. The election results in Saxony-Anhalt also seem to reflect this.

Political scientist Sven Leunig from the Friedrich Schiller University Jena in the state of Thuringia has his own take on the reaction of eastern Germans, especially after the Leipzig incident. 

"It is less a fundamental rejection of support for Ukraine, more a reaction based on fear," Leunig said. "They want to keep out of the conflict, so as not to be drawn further into it. That of course strengthens parties like the AfD, BSW and Left, who accommodate these sentiments."

Support for Ukraine is also coming under pressure for another reason. According to the AfD and BSW, the money Ukraine receives could be better spent on Germany's stretched social services. AfD lawmaker Gottfried Curio, for example, accused the German government of cutting social benefits and raising taxes "to keep on giving billions to foreign countries," to finance "foreign wars" such as in Ukraine.

Support for Ukraine is crumbling, but slowly

Chancellor Merz still believes he has political and public backing for his course. During the Bundestag debate, this was his response to the AfD's suggestion of resuming energy deliveries from Russia and ending German support for Ukraine: "This path that you depict is not supported by the majority in the German parliament and it is also not supported by the majority of the population of the Federal Republic of Germany. We will defend our freedom, also in the future."

But support for Ukraine, as shown in ARD Deutschlandtrend surveys over the years, is becoming less favored by the public. The share of people who think military support goes too far is growing, slowly but steadily, and is now 42%.

Leunig thinks the German government is not yet under pressure to reconsider its Ukraine policy: it still has "clear support" for the current course. "Plus, the threat coming from Russia is also becoming widely recognized. Of course, if public support weakens in the long-term, the government will have to react to that."

Is Ukraine 'another Afghanistan'?

His colleague Johannes Varwick, on the other hand, advises a course correction now, but not so much due to the mood in Germany: "Yes, we should stand with Ukraine, but standing by Ukraine does not mean fueling a futile war of attrition without a viable political strategy. That runs Ukraine into the ground, even if it is portrayed as 'pro-Ukraine'."

Critics have drawn parallels to Western intervention in Afghanistan, which after 20 years, billions of dollars spent and about 3500 western soldiers killed, ended with the Taliban retaking power.

But Leunig sees it differently. "I think both cases are not identical. In Afghanistan there was a direct military intervention by Western countries with ground and air forces. In Ukraine, the support is supplying weapons. But the public fear that the war will drag on for a long time, in this there is of course a parallel to Afghanistan, and that in the end Ukraine might still have to give up."

So far, however, there is no sign that the German government is rethinking its position. During a recent (September 10) visit from NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte in Berlin, German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul said, "Germany will stay the course during this time," despite the domestic debate.

This article was translated from German.

entries.title: The Crusades: How a medieval Holy War still shapes politics
entries.summary: In 1095, the Catholic Church launched the Crusades: wars that left millions dead and whose legacy still shapes political and ideological conflicts.
entries.content:
September 14, 2026

In 1095, the Catholic Church launched the Crusades: wars that left millions dead and whose legacy still shapes political and ideological conflicts.

"The present moment is much like the 11th century. ... We don't want to fight, but, like our fellow Christians a thousand years ago, we must." Those are the words of US Secretary of War Pete Hegseth in his 2020 book, "American Crusade: Our Fight to Stay Free."  

Hegseth has repeatedly used the biblical language and symbolism of the Crusades to frame both domestic and foreign policy, from the current war in Iran to the "fight" against the "scourge of leftism."  

Nearly 1,000 years have passed since the November day in 1095 when Pope Urban II delivered the fiery speech that would ignite centuries of warfare and change the course of history.

But Hegseth is only the latest in a long line of politicians and extremists to reference the Crusades — from the Ku Klux Klan to US President George W. Bush and Osama bin Laden.  

Why do the Crusades remain such a powerful source of inspiration for contemporary leaders?

Princes and peasants promised eternal salvation

The history of the Crusades is long and complex. But it can be summarized as an extraordinary example of how religion can become a powerful tool for political goals, helping leaders to unite people, justify wars and mobilize support on a massive scale.

In the mid-11th century, Muslim Seljuk Turks conquered vast swaths of territory in the Middle East. In the early 1070s, they took control of Jerusalem, the most important holy site in Christendom. Rumors spread that pilgrims and Christians living in the region were being persecuted, and holy sites desecrated.

The papacy in Rome at the time was locked in a bitter power struggle with Holy Roman Emperor Henry IV over who really held the reins of power in Western Christendom. When Byzantine Emperor Alexios I Komnenos appealed to Pope Urban II for help to defend against the Seljuks in 1095, it presented the papacy with an opportunity to demonstrate its power by bypassing Henry to rally Europe's nobility for nothing less than Holy War.

Urban believed that a major Christian cause would strengthen his authority by uniting Western Europe toward a common external enemy.

War was the status quo in medieval Europe, which had been hit by a series of droughts, famines and plagues. Belief in the "end times" was widespread.

In this context, Urban's call for a Holy War to "liberate the Church of God" was persuasive: He demonized Muslims and promised Crusaders complete forgiveness for all past sins — as well as eternal salvation.

"If you think about what a Crusade is, it's asking people to go into the unknown, thousands of miles into an unknown land," said Jonathan Phillips, an expert on crusading history at Royal Holloway University in London. Their chances of dying were about 35% to 40%, he said. So they had "to be driven by something. Religion has to come at the top," he added.

Urban's call to Holy War was taken up by men and women from every level of society, from "princes to peasants," Phillips said. A "tabby cat army," as he describes it, composed of peasants, low-ranking knights and nobles, and led by preachers, set out for the Holy Land in 1096.

This would later become known as the People's Crusade, which claimed its first victims in the Rhineland, where Jewish communities were massacred in one of medieval Europe's earliest outbreaks of antisemitism. 

A better-organized army of European upper nobility was eventually assembled in Constantinople between November 1096 and April 1097.

Unprecedented bloodshed

The Holy Land, located between what is today Turkey, Syria and Egypt, was a polyglot society divided among Sunni Seljuk Turkish warlords and the Shi'a Fatimid Caliphate. 

It took some time for locals to understand that this wasn't just another raid, said Mohamad El-Merheb, an expert on the premodern Islamic Eastern Mediterranean at SOAS University of London: "It takes maybe at least a decade for some people to see it as an ideological project to convert and take the Holy Land."

"Some of the cities are well defended, some are not. But it is all in the context of very fragmented political power," El-Merheb said.

The Crusaders had what El-Merheb describes as a series of swift conquests in important cities such as Edessa and Antioch. Despite these early victories, life fighting a Holy War was grueling. The majority returned home, or died of disease, hunger or sheer exhaustion.

When they captured Jerusalem in 1099, Crusaders massacred thousands of Muslims and Jews because they couldn't tell them apart.

Many historians consider the fall of the city of Acre to Mamluk warriors in 1291 to be the end of the Crusades in the Holy Land.

Later crusades were also called, however, including to block the advance of Ottoman Turks in Eastern Europe in 14th century. "Reconquista" Christian military campaigns aimed to retake the Iberian Peninsula from Muslim rule into the late 15th century.

The Crusades meet the culture wars

The legacy of the Crusades remains a powerful and polarizing cultural touchstone. In both the East and the West, the historical memory of these medieval holy wars is frequently repurposed to frame modern identities, politics and conflicts.

In 2001, US President George W. Bush caused uproar when he described the so-called "War on Terror" as a "crusade," a term already used by Osama bin Laden to frame US-led wars as religious wars intended to destroy Islam. 

In his propaganda to legitimize his global jihad, bin Laden also invoked the legacy of Saladin, a legendary Kurdish commander revered to this day as the hero who recaptured Jerusalem from the Crusaders in 1187.

"As of the 19th century, Saladin specifically becomes a symbol of fighting Western colonialism and imperialism," said El-Merheb. "Throughout the 20th century, a lot of Islamist groups also start referring to the Western powers as Crusaders, so this becomes part of political nationalism on the state level and also on a more popular level in films, for example. This is happening in the West now in the opposite way." 

Crusader symbolism has long been used by far-right movements in the United States and Europe to promote narratives of civilizational conflict. The Latin phrase "deus vult," or "God wills it," has been used by figures including far-right mass murderer Anders Breivik and Germany's far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) party, while France's far-right party Reconquête draws its name from the Reconquista campaigns. US Secretary of War Pete Hegseth famously has "deus vult" tattooed on his arm and a Crusader cross on his chest. 

But El-Merheb believes that such references often reduce the Crusades to a simple clash between Christianity and Islam, "which really was never simply the case."

This framing, he said, ignores "how the Crusades were from the start very antisemitic projects, or violent projects against other Christian communities in Europe such as the Cathars in France, against Byzantium and the Islamic world and ignores the many cross-religious alliances between Muslims and Crusaders."

Along the way, he said, these politicians are also forgetting how violent and destructive these historical campaigns were.

Edited by: Elizabeth Grenier

entries.title: Nepal: thousands still missing as flood recovery begins
entries.summary: The Himalayan nation is moving from rescue operations to recovery, facing a $4.8 billion reconstruction bill amid renewed calls for climate justice.
entries.content:
Nepal

Nepal: thousands still missing as flood recovery begins

September 14, 2026

The Himalayan nation is moving from rescue operations to recovery, facing a $4.8 billion reconstruction bill amid renewed calls for climate justice.

Nearly three weeks after deadly flash floods swept through Nepal's Bhotekoshi-Trishuli river corridor near the Chinese border, the Himalayan nation is shifting from search-and-rescue operations to relief and reconstruction efforts.

Authorities in Nepal say at least 1,386 bodies have been recovered across five affected districts, while more than 5,130 people are still missing. The latter figure includes 587 foreign nationals and around 900 workers employed in hydropower tunnels and other energy facilities.

The deluge, which authorities say was triggered by a glacier collapse, devastated communities and swept away more than a dozen hydropower facilities. As search operations continue in submerged tunnels and along muddy riverbanks, families are growing increasingly desperate for news of missing loved ones.

Villages wiped out in minutes

The scale of human loss is particularly stark in the upper river basins, where entire settlements vanished within minutes. In many places, destroyed roads and bridges have cut off access, forcing rescue and relief teams to rely on helicopters to deliver essential supplies.

Niranjan Paudyal, a resident of Sole village in Nepal's Nuwakot District who lost his parents, uncle, aunt and sister in the flash floods, said the flood took away even the chance of burying his family members.

"We spent days searching through debris, hoping for signs of my missing parents and family," he told DW. "Sadly, the disaster left us with no choice but to perform their final rites without their bodies."

Public land in Uttargaya Rural Municipality in Rasuwa District has either been washed away or rendered unsafe.

"There is not even land left after the flood to perform the final rites of those who lost their lives," Chameli Gurung, the municipality's deputy chair, told DW. "Relatives have to travel to Kathmandu's Pashupati Aryaghat to perform the final rites."

In Uttargaya alone, at least 618 houses were swept away or buried and 877 people remain missing. Only 12 bodies have been recovered. Gurung said local authorities are exploring the possibility of leasing private land to accommodate displaced families before winter.

Nepal's communication minister, Bikram Timilsina, told DW that affected people are being resettled close to their original homes by securing nearby public or private land and providing financial assistance based on household size until they can become self-reliant.

Nepal faced with a colossal recovery bill

As emergency relief efforts begin to stabilize, Nepal faces a massive financial burden. A preliminary rapid damage and needs assessment (RDNA) puts the total reconstruction requirement at about 723.3 billion Nepalese rupees ($4.78 billion, €4.1 billion), according to local media reports.

The RDNA estimates that nearly two thirds of the funds will go into restoring energy and transport networks and academic facilities.

Hydropower, which supplies almost all of ⁠Nepal's electricity, had become a fast-growing source of the country's export revenue. The flood damage has deepened concerns about how Nepal will finance its recovery.

On Monday, neighboring India approved the export of power to Nepal for 18 hours a day until at least December 31, Reuters news agency reported.

"We will try to utilize all of our domestic resources and seek international support to manage the funding gaps," Timilsina, the communication minister, told DW.

Nepal wants to grow resilient

Nepal has formally approached the UN Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC)-backed Loss and Damage Fund for assistance. However, the fund, established to help countries deal with the impacts of climate change, has yet to begin distributing its limited resources.

Nepal is seeking to turn reconstruction into part of a broader economic recovery strategy, with an emphasis on climate-resilient infrastructure rather than simply replacing what was destroyed.

"Given our previous experience with post-disaster management, what matters most is how effectively we can use the funds to restore lives and livelihoods and build disaster-resilient infrastructure," Roshee Lamichhane, an associate professor at Kathmandu University, told DW.

Demand for climate justice

Beyond recovery finance, Nepal is making a broader climate justice argument on the international stage.

Nepal's Prime Minister Balendra Shah is scheduled to address the United Nations General Assembly in New York on September 24, where he is expected to call for global responsibility for mitigating climate impacts.

Despite contributing less than 0.1% of global greenhouse gas emissions, Nepal remains highly vulnerable to climate-induced hazards.

"Reconstruction would be used as an opportunity to build climate-resilient infrastructure," Maheshwar Dhakal, who leads the Climate Change Management Division at Nepal's Ministry of Forests and Environment, told DW. "We will develop a guideline with the motto of 'tomorrow for a better future.'"

Climate scientists caution against attributing any single extreme event solely to global warming without detailed studies, but they agree that rising temperatures are accelerating glacial melt across the Himalayas.

Manjeet Dhakal, director of Climate Analytics South Asia, says the scale of the disaster highlights the growing consequences of rising global temperatures and gives Nepal an opportunity to advocate for cuts in global carbon emissions on the international stage.

"How many more disasters should we wait for before there is a global response to address the impacts of climate change?" he asked, adding that developed and advanced countries, alongside other nations, should take greater responsibility.

Edited by: Keith Walker

entries.title: EU leaders urge unity after Russian strike on train
entries.summary: Russia's drone attack on a train near the Ukraine-Poland border has triggered EU calls to up support for Kyiv. Allies of Ukraine should show they "are not scared," said the bloc's top diplomat, Kaja Kallas.
entries.content:
Ukraine

EU leaders urge unity after Russian strike on train

September 14, 2026

Russia's drone attack on a train near the Ukraine-Poland border has triggered EU calls to up support for Kyiv. Allies of Ukraine should show they "are not scared," said the bloc's top diplomat, Kaja Kallas.

Several top EU politicians have called a Russian drone strike on a passenger train ​on Ukraine's border with Poland a bid by Moscow to intimidate Kyiv's allies that should be met with even more resolution.

In the incident, a drone hit the train's locomotive at a railway station in the Volyn region, some 2 kilometers (1.24 miles) from the border, shortly after a diplomatic ‌train carrying former British ​Prime ⁠Minister Boris Johnson and other ⁠European ​diplomats had been at the station.

What did EU leaders say about the train attack?

"It [the attack] is clearly meant to scare Western countries from supporting Ukraine, from going to Ukraine to show support," the EU's foreign policy chief, Kaja Kallas, said.

"I ​think we should act the opposite. ​We should show that we are ⁠there ​for Ukraine ​and we are ​not scared," ‌she told reporters in ​Finland, ⁠where she attended ⁠a ​summit on Arctic strategy.

Finnish Prime Minister Petteri Orpo, who was also at the meeting, said the attack demonstrated Russia's growing aggression and called both for more support for Kyiv and for harsher penalties on Moscow.

"For me, it means that we have to [...] do even more to help Ukraine, to support Ukraine. And we need more measures against Russia, more political measures, more sanctions, and make it clear that this is strong strategy," he said.

"We are united here in Europe," he added.

Lithuanian President Gitanas Nauseda said the attack showed that Russia was "challenging all of us."

"We should not talk about concrete geographic regions, because Russia's goal is much more ambitious: to test the rule of law, to test our style of life, to test democracy. And I think they will put additional efforts to do it," he said.

French Foreign Affairs Minister Jean-Noel Barrot said the attack had a "very clear goal, which is to intimidate Europeans, discourage them and, above all, drive a wedge between them."

Barrot said Russian President Vladimir Putin had constantly stepped up pressure on the EU and NATO over the past five years.

"Why? Because he knows that our strength lies in our unity, and that as long as we stand together, nothing can intimidate us," he said.

Germany warns against escalation with Russia

German Foreign Minister Boris Pistorius, for his part, called for caution.

"I take the drones that were approaching trains near the (Ukrainian-Polish) border very seriously, but we must not be forced into an escalation," he said.

The Kremlin has commented on the attack only by saying that the Russian army operated across all Ukrainian territory and would continue to do so.

Speaking about the incident on Sunday, Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andriy Sybiga has said Putin considered Russia to be "de facto" at war with Europe.

"Putin's terror is literally knocking at the door of the European Union and NATO," Sybiga said.

NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte said Russia's attack would drive the transatlantic alliance to keep on pushing its support for Ukraine.

“Russia is growing increasingly reckless as it continues its terrible war against Ukraine," Rutte said at NATO's offices in Brussels, adding a call to increase support for Kyiv.

According to Rutte, Russian leader Putin "thinks he can stop" NATO from supporting Ukraine.

"He is wrong."

Edited by: Natalie Muller
